name: Context Windows and Long Context
intent: Understand what the context window limits, what a long prompt costs in time and memory, and why a bigger window does not mean the model uses all of it well.
scenario: A law firm wants an assistant that answers questions about a 300-page contract. The text is far longer than a typical prompt, and the team must choose between a model with a very large window and cutting the document down.
problem: A model can only use what is inside its context window: the prompt, the earlier conversation, any documents and the answer it is writing, all counted in tokens. Anything outside the window does not exist for the model. Making the window larger helps, but a long prompt costs more at every step: more attention work, more memory for the keys and values of every token, and more money per call. And a model does not necessarily use a long context evenly.

howItWorks.title: The window is a budget of tokens
howItWorks.text: Every model has a maximum length for the prompt and the answer together, measured in tokens. Some services also cap the answer separately. Text that does not fit has to be cut, summarised or left out, and the model cannot see what was dropped.

howItWorks.title: Chat history is resent each turn
howItWorks.text: A model has no memory between calls. A chat application sends the earlier messages again with every new one, so a long conversation fills the window and makes each call bigger, slower and more expensive even when the new message is short.

howItWorks.title: Attention work grows with the square of the length
howItWorks.text: While the prompt is read, each token is scored against the earlier ones, so doubling the prompt roughly quadruples that part of the work. Services pass this on as higher latency before the first word, and often as a higher price for very long prompts.

howItWorks.title: Memory grows with every token
howItWorks.text: While generating, the model keeps the keys and values of every token in the KV cache. For an example model with 32 layers, 8 key-value heads of size 128 and 16-bit numbers, that is 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131072 bytes, or 128 KiB, for each token of each request. A full 8192-token window needs 1 GiB for one request.

howItWorks.title: Using the window well is a separate problem
howItWorks.text: In the 'Lost in the Middle' study, the models tested were best at using information at the start or the end of the context and worse at information in the middle, and long-context models still became less accurate as the input grew. Results differ between models and change over time, so test your own task and your own model.

howItWorks.title: Put less in, on purpose
howItWorks.text: Retrieval selects the few passages that matter instead of sending the whole document. Older conversation can be summarised. A long fixed prefix can be cached. Important instructions and facts can be placed at the start or the end. All of these keep the prompt short and relevant.

pros: A large window lets one request see a whole contract, codebase or conversation
It removes the need to split and merge for documents that fit
It makes simple prototypes easy: paste everything in
It can reduce the number of moving parts, such as a retriever, at small scale
cons: Cost and latency grow with prompt length, and attention work grows faster than the length
KV cache memory per request grows with every token, which limits how many requests fit on a GPU
Accuracy can fall for information deep inside a long prompt, and the model may ignore parts of it
Each call resends the same context unless the service caches the prefix
whenToUse: The whole input really is needed at once, such as summarising one document that fits
You are sizing memory and cost for a feature that sends long prompts
You are choosing between a bigger window and retrieval for a large body of text
whenNotToUse: Do not paste a whole knowledge base into every prompt: retrieve the few passages that matter
Do not assume a long window means perfect recall of everything in it
Do not rely on a chat history that grows without limit: trim or summarise it
pitfalls: Counting words instead of tokens and discovering the overflow in production
Forgetting that the answer also uses the window, so a full prompt leaves no room for it
Sending the same long instructions on every call without caching them
Putting the one key fact in the middle of a very long prompt and not testing that it is used

roles.label: Prompt and history
roles.description: Instructions, earlier messages and documents, all counted in tokens.

roles.label: Context window
roles.description: The maximum number of tokens the model can take in one request, answer included.

roles.label: KV cache
roles.description: The keys and values of every token so far, kept in GPU memory while the model generates.

roles.label: Answer
roles.description: The tokens the model writes. They use the same window as the prompt.

sources.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

quiz.question: A 300-page contract is about 150,000 tokens. The assistant's model has a 128,000-token window. What is the best design?
options: Cut the contract at 128,000 tokens and tell users that the end of it is not covered
Ask users to split the contract into two files and upload each one separately
Retrieve the sections that matter for each question, and send those with the question
Switch to the model with the largest window available, whatever it costs per call
quiz.explanation: Most questions need only a few passages, and a short prompt is faster, cheaper and easier for the model to use well. Cutting the end loses content silently, splitting makes users do the work, and the largest window still pays for every token on every call and may use the middle poorly.

quiz.question: A chatbot resends the whole conversation with each message. After 30 turns each call is slow and costly, although the user's new message is only a sentence. What is the best fix?
options: Summarise or trim the older turns, and cache the fixed prefix where the service allows it
Ask the model to answer more briefly, so that the replies add fewer tokens to the history
Remove the system instructions from every call after the first one, to save tokens
Increase the temperature so that the model spends less time deciding on each answer
quiz.explanation: The cost comes from the growing history that is sent every time. Summarising old turns keeps the prompt short, and caching a fixed prefix avoids paying for the same tokens again. Shorter replies help only a little, dropping instructions changes behaviour, and temperature does not affect prompt length.

quiz.question: A model advertises a 128,000-token window. A colleague says that this means it will use every part of a 128,000-token prompt equally well. What is the best response?
options: Correct, because the model reads every token with the same attention weight
Correct, as long as the prompt is below the limit, since the window guarantees recall
Incorrect, because the window only limits the answer, not the prompt
Incorrect: a window says what fits, and studies found that models can use information in the middle of a long prompt less well, so test it
quiz.explanation: The window is a limit on what can be sent, not a promise about how well it is used. The 'Lost in the Middle' study found weaker use of information in the middle of long inputs for the models it tested. Results vary by model, so measure on your own task.
